author_claim: The Hebrew construct phrase קִלְלַת אֱלֹהִים in Deuteronomy 21:23 contains a grammatical ambiguity, allowing אֱלֹהִים to be rendered either as a subjective genitive ('accursed in the sight of God') or an objective genitive ('an insult or reproach against God').
short_quote: The ambiguity arises out of the construction of
source_locator: Excursus: 'The interpretation of Deut. xxi. 23', p. 152 (PDF derivative p. 54)
qualification: Lightfoot notes that Hebrew grammar admits both subjective (Judg 9:57) and objective (Gen 27:13) genitives, giving rise to two distinct interpretive traditions.
notes: Visibly verified on printed p. 152. Pinned to Prompt 2 citation index 0.

author_claim: Paul follows the Septuagint rendering of Deuteronomy 21:23 in substance, but instinctively omits ὑπὸ Θεοῦ in Galatians 3:13 because Christ was not personally a sinner subject to divine wrath, but rather voluntarily bore the vicarious curse on humanity's behalf (γενόμενος ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν κατάρα).
short_quote: and St Paul instinctively omits those words which do not strictly apply
source_locator: Commentary on Galatians 3:13, p. 140 (PDF derivative p. 42)
qualification: Lightfoot explicitly qualifies that if ὑπὸ Θεοῦ had been retained, it would have required theological qualification since the curse of the law rests on the sinner, whereas Christ was sinless. Self-audit correction incorporated.
notes: Visibly verified on printed p. 140. Pinned to Prompt 2 citation index 4.

author_claim: The objective genitive rendering ('he that hangeth is a reproach or insult against God') became the popular Jewish and Ebionite interpretation from the second century onward to ward off the reproach of a crucified Messiah and turn the passage against persecutors.
short_quote: This seems to have been the popular Jewish interpretation
source_locator: Excursus: 'The interpretation of Deut. xxi. 23', pp. 152-153 (PDF derivative pp. 54-55)
qualification: Lightfoot traces this shift through Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, the Targum of Pseudo-Jonathan, Siphri, Ariston of Pella, and Jerome's account of Ebionite interpretation.
notes: Visibly verified on printed pp. 152-153. Pinned to Prompt 2 citation index 14.

author_claim: Although Deuteronomy 21:23 originally contemplated post-mortem impalement or exposure rather than death by crucifixion, Paul's application of the passage to Christ's crucifixion is entirely legitimate because Jewish law and tradition attached the ignominy and curse to the hanging itself.
short_quote: did not contemplate death by crucifixion, the application was quite legitimate
source_locator: Excursus: 'The interpretation of Deut. xxi. 23', p. 154 (PDF derivative p. 56)
qualification: Lightfoot notes that ancient Jewish usage (Chaldee paraphrase, Peshitta Syriac, and the rabbinic epithet תלוי) applied the Deuteronomy phrase indiscriminately to hanging after execution and to crucifixion.
notes: Visibly verified on printed p. 154. Pinned to Prompt 2 citation index 20.

author_claim: In Genesis 15:6, the Hebrew text reads וַיַּחְשְׁבֶהָ לּוֹ צְדָקָה with an active verb ('and He imputed it to him for righteousness'), whereas Paul quotes the Septuagint passive ἐλογίσθη verbatim in both Galatians 3:6 and Romans 4:3, agreeing also with James 2:23 and Clement of Rome.
short_quote: It is quoted as in the Lxx also in Rom. iv. 3
source_locator: Commentary on Galatians 3:6, p. 136 (PDF derivative p. 38)
qualification: Lightfoot notes Barnabas § 13 quotes the passage too loosely with an obvious Pauline infusion to serve as an independent text-critical witness.
notes: Visibly verified on printed p. 136. Substantive cross-epistle comparison connecting Gal 3:6 and Rom 4:3. Pinned to Prompt 2 citation index 25.

author_claim: By the time of the Christian era, Genesis 15:6 had become a standard text in both Alexandrian and Rabbinic schools, providing a shared theological foundation that prepared the way for apostolic teaching on faith.
short_quote: standard text in the Jewish schools
source_locator: Excursus: 'The Faith of Abraham', p. 159 (PDF derivative p. 61)
qualification: Lightfoot emphasizes that while both Alexandrian and Palestinian schools recognized the centrality of Gen 15:6, the doctrinal lessons they deduced from it were widely divergent.
notes: Visibly verified on printed p. 159. Pinned to Prompt 2 citation index 30.

author_claim: Philo comments on Genesis 15:6 at least ten times, extolling Abraham's faith as the queen of virtues, but allegorizes his history as the individual soul's philosophical journey toward God rather than a covenantal community.
short_quote: To him it was not a history, but an allegory
source_locator: Excursus: 'The Faith of Abraham', pp. 159-160 (PDF derivative pp. 61-62)
qualification: Lightfoot notes Philo fully grasped the personal aspect of faith but lacked any conception of a corporate Church or covenant people of God.
notes: Visibly verified on printed pp. 159-160. Pinned to Prompt 2 citation index 35.

author_claim: Early Rabbinic tradition in the Mechilta on Exodus 14:31 treated Abraham's faith in Genesis 15:6 as a meritorious work earning both worlds for his posterity, while later Jewish commentators reversed the grammatical subject to 'Abraham counted on God's righteousness' to counter Christian justification theology.
short_quote: by the merit of faith whereby he believed
source_locator: Excursus: 'The Faith of Abraham', pp. 162-164 (PDF derivative pp. 64-66)
qualification: Lightfoot observes that later Jewish polemic inverted the biblical sense of Gen 15:6 specifically to evade Paul's inference of justification by faith.
notes: Visibly verified on printed pp. 162-164. Pinned to Prompt 2 citation index 43.

author_claim: The apparent contradiction between Paul (Gal 3:6 / Rom 4:3) and James (Jas 2:23) regarding Genesis 15:6 resolves because they independently targeted different perversions—Paul confronting Pharisaic legalism and James confronting barren orthodoxy—while leaving open whether James wrote with direct awareness of Paul's language.
short_quote: destroy the force of any argument founded on the mere coincidence
source_locator: Excursus: 'The Faith of Abraham', p. 164 (PDF derivative p. 66)
qualification: Lightfoot maintains that Paul and James are fundamentally harmonious, but explicitly qualifies that whether James knew Paul's epistles or was addressing independent Jewish errors cannot be dogmatically decided. Self-audit correction incorporated.
notes: Visibly verified on printed p. 164. Pinned to Prompt 2 citation index 48.

author_claim: In Galatians 2:21, the verb ἀθετῶ means 'to nullify' or 'to set at nought,' matching its lexical usage in 1 Corinthians 1:19 and Luke 7:30, with its contextual meaning fixed by δωρεὰν ἀπέθανεν.
source_locator: Commentary on Galatians 2:21, p. 120 (PDF derivative p. 22)
qualification: Passing lexical cross-reference; Lightfoot does not comment on the quotation of Isaiah 29:14 or its Old Testament context.
notes: Visibly verified on printed p. 120. Pinned to Prompt 2 citation index 53.

author_claim: The Septuagint adopted the subjective genitive (κεκατηραμένος ὑπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ), whereas later Greek versions (Aquila κατάρα Θεοῦ, Symmachus propter blasphemiam Dei), the Targum of Pseudo-Jonathan, and the Peshitta adopted the objective genitive ('an insult/blasphemy against God').
source_locator: Excursus: 'The interpretation of Deut. xxi. 23', pp. 152-153 (PDF derivative pp. 54-55)
qualification: Lightfoot details how early versions split between subjective divine curse and objective blasphemy/contempt against God.
notes: Visibly verified on printed pp. 152-153. Pinned to Prompt 7 citation index 12.

author_claim: Deuteronomy 21:23 occupied a prominent place in Jewish-Christian polemics, cited against Christian faith by Jewish opponents in Justin Martyr's Dialogue with Trypho (§§ 95-96), Ariston of Pella's Dispute of Jason and Papiscus, Tertullian (Adv. Judaeos § 10), and Jerome.
short_quote: This passage occupied an important place in the early controversies
source_locator: Excursus: 'The interpretation of Deut. xxi. 23', pp. 152-153 (PDF derivative pp. 54-55)
qualification: Lightfoot notes how early Christian apologists consistently followed Paul in turning the curse into a vicarious redemption.
notes: Visibly verified on printed pp. 152-153. Pinned to Prompt 7 citation index 5.

author_claim: In the Dialogue with Trypho § 96, Justin Martyr quotes both Deuteronomy 27:26 and 21:23 with the exact distinctive Pauline adaptations found in Galatians 3:10 and 3:13 (omitting ὑπὸ Θεοῦ and adding πᾶς and ἐπὶ ξύλου), demonstrating his reliance on Paul's epistle.
short_quote: applies them as they are applied in Gal. iii. 10, 13
source_locator: Introduction § V: 'Genuineness of the Epistle', pp. 60-61 (PDF derivative pp. 16-17)
qualification: Text-critical proof that Justin Martyr drew directly from the text of Galatians 3:13 rather than independently citing the Septuagint.
notes: Visibly verified on printed pp. 60-61. Pinned to Prompt 7 citation index 24.
